steps.body:
Nothing labels the inside for you. Two questions decide it:

**What is inside something?** (a bracket, a root, an exponent, a denominator)
**Is its derivative also present, up to a constant?**

If both answers are yes, that thing is u. If the second answer is no, substitution will not save you — and in this course, that means the integral is out of reach.

explanationVariants: The inside is x³ + 1, whose derivative 3x² is present (up to the constant 3 — and the x² out front is a third of it).
Ask what is inside the bracket, then check that its derivative is available.

widget.prompt: For ∫ x²(x³ + 1)⁵ dx, what is u?

options.label: u = x³ + 1; du = 3x² dx supplies the x² factor.
options.feedback: Right. The x² is a third of the du, and a constant like that is always fixable out front.

options.label: u = x²; its derivative supplies the x² factor.
options.feedback: x² is not INSIDE anything. It is the leftover factor — the receipt — and it is what becomes the du.

options.label: u = x³; its derivative makes the power disappear.
options.feedback: Very close, and it would even work here (du = 3x² dx again). But taking the whole inside, x³ + 1, keeps the bracket clean as u⁵.

options.label: No substitution can match both the factor and the power.
options.feedback: There is: the inside is x³ + 1 and its derivative 3x² is sitting right there, up to a constant.

explanationVariants: Check by differentiating (x³ + 1)⁶/18: the chain rule gives 6(x³+1)⁵·3x²/18 = x²(x³+1)⁵ ✓.

commonErrors.feedback: The 1/3 from x² dx = du/3 has gone missing: 63/6 = 10.5 is three times too big.
That is 64/18 — you forgot to subtract the lower limit, u = 1, whose sixth power is 1.
That looks like (64 − 1)/54 — one division too many. It is (1/3)(u⁶/6) = u⁶/18.

panels.title: The inside is there
panels.body: u = x² + 1 looks tempting. It is genuinely the inside of the bracket.

panels.title: But the du is not
panels.body: du = 2x dx, and there is NO x out front to supply it. You cannot manufacture one — dividing by 2x would move a VARIABLE across the integral sign, which is illegal.

panels.title: So expand instead
panels.body: (x² + 1)³ = x⁶ + 3x⁴ + 3x² + 1, and now the power rule handles it term by term. Substitution is a tool, not an obligation — and knowing when it does NOT apply is half of using it well.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the second panel is the whole test.
widget.successFeedback: No inner derivative, no substitution. Constants may cross the integral sign; variables may not.

steps.body:
And that is integration, in this course.

You can **define** an integral (the trap, squeezed shut), **interpret** it (a rate integrated gives a total), **compute** it (an antiderivative, evaluated twice), and **transform** it (substitution, the chain rule reversed).

What remains is not new machinery but new uses: areas between curves, volumes, average values. Those are the next course.

explanationVariants: Substitution works exactly when the inner derivative is present up to a CONSTANT factor. A stray x that is not part of the du is fatal.
The test is mechanical: write down du and ask whether the integrand supplies it.

widget.prompt: For which of these does u-substitution work?

items.label: ∫ 2x·cos(x²) dx
items.feedback: u = x², du = 2x dx — sitting right there. The integral becomes ∫cos u du = sin(x²) + C.

items.label: ∫ cos(x²) dx
items.feedback: u = x² needs du = 2x dx, and there is no x. You cannot conjure one, and in fact this integral has no elementary antiderivative at all.

items.label: ∫ x·e^(x²) dx
items.feedback: u = x², du = 2x dx, and x dx = du/2. A constant is always fixable.

items.label: ∫ (x + 1)⁵ dx
items.feedback: u = x + 1, du = dx. The simplest substitution there is — and it works because the inner derivative is 1.

widget.missFeedback: Write down du and ask: does the integrand supply it, up to a constant?
widget.successFeedback: Constants can be fixed; a missing VARIABLE cannot. That single test settles every case.

hints: What is inside something? The exponent, x². And is its derivative there? There is an x out front — half of 2x.
u = x², du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2. The limits become u: 0 → 1.
explanationVariants: Check by differentiating e^(x²)/2: the chain rule gives e^(x²)·2x/2 = x·e^(x²) ✓.

widget.prompt: ∫₀¹ x·e^(x²) dx, as a decimal to three places. (e ≈ 2.71828)

commonErrors.feedback: That is e − 1 without the ½ from x dx = du/2.
That is e/2. You must subtract e⁰ = 1 as well: (e − 1)/2 = 0.859.
That is the ½ alone. It multiplies (e − 1) ≈ 1.718, giving 0.859.

steps.body: Two questions, and you are done.
takeaways: What is inside something? Is its derivative present, up to a constant? If both, that is your u.
Constants may be moved across the integral sign. Variables may not — which is why a missing x is fatal.
Substitution is a tool, not an obligation: knowing when it fails (∫cos(x²) dx) is half of using it well.
steps.teaser: That is integration. Next course: what to DO with it — areas between curves, volumes, and average value.

concept.body: Write down the candidate u, then immediately write du. Now look at the integrand: **does it contain that du, up to a constant?** If yes, substitute. If a bare x is left over, stop — that substitution is the wrong one.

explanationVariants: u = x² needs du = 2x dx. In ∫ x·sin(x²) dx there IS an x, so x dx = du/2 and it works.
In ∫ sin(x²) dx there is no x at all, and the substitution dies.

widget.prompt: Which one can be done by substitution?

options.label: ∫ x·sin(x²) dx
options.feedback: Right — the x supplies the du, up to a factor of ½.

options.label: ∫ sin(x²) dx
options.feedback: There is no x to become the du, and you cannot manufacture one. This integral has no elementary antiderivative at all.
